content: Sweet Flag Calamus, also known as Common Sweet Flag (Acorus calamus), is a plant belonging to the Acoraceae family and the Acorus genus. It is a tall, perennial wetland monocot with aromatic leaves and rhizomes. These rhizomes have been historically used for medicinal purposes, for their fragrance, and as a psychotropic substance. The plant is known by various names, including cinnamon sedge, flagroot, gladdon, myrtle flag, myrtle grass, myrtle sedge, sweet cane, sweet myrtle, sweet root, sweet rush, and sweet sedge. Acorus calamus is believed to have originated in India but is now distributed across Europe, southern Russia, northern Asia Minor, southern Siberia, China, Japan, Burma, Sri Lanka, and northern parts of the United States. Botanical Information The morphological distinction between Acorus species is based on the number of prominent leaf veins. Acorus calamus is characterized by a single prominent midvein, flanked by slightly raised secondary veins (less than half the diameter of the midvein) and numerous fine tertiary veins. This feature differentiates it from Acorus americanus. The leaves of Acorus calamus are sympodial and slightly shorter than the vegetative leaves, with curly or undulate margins. The flowers are longer, measuring between 3 and 4 mm, compared to other species. Acorus calamus is infertile, exhibiting an abortive ovary with a shriveled appearance. Chemistry Both triploid and tetraploid varieties of Acorus calamus contain asarone, a chemical compound, whereas the diploid variety does not contain any asarone. Regulations In 1968, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) banned the use of calamus and its derivatives, such as calamus oil, as food additives and medicines. Usage Acorus calamus has been a traded commodity in various cultures for thousands of years. Medicinally, it has been used to treat a wide range of ailments. In ancient times, particularly in the Orient and Egypt, the rhizome was considered a potent aphrodisiac. In Europe, Acorus calamus was often added to wine, and its root is thought to have been one of the possible ingredients in absinthe. Among northern Native American tribes, the plant was used both medicinally and as a stimulant. Additionally, the root was believed to have been used as an entheogen by these communities. At high doses, it exhibits hallucinogenic properties. Cultural Symbolism The calamus plant has long been a symbol of male love. Its name is associated with a Greek myth involving Kalamos, the son of the river god Maeander, who loved Karpos, the son of Zephyrus and Chloris. When Karpos drowned, Kalamos was transformed into a reed, whose rustling in the wind was interpreted as a lamentation. The plant was a favorite of Henry David Thoreau, who referred to it as sweet flag, and Walt Whitman, who included a section called The Calamus Poems in the third edition of Leaves of Grass (1860). In these poems, the calamus symbolizes love, lust, and affection. Some interpretations suggest that this symbolism derives from the visual resemblance of the plant's spadix to the erect human penis. The name Sweet Flag refers to the plant's sweet scent (it was historically used as a strewing herb) and the wavy edges of its leaves, which resemble a fluttering flag. In Japan, the plant symbolizes the bravery of samurai due to its sharp, sword-like leaves. Even today, families with young boys celebrate the Boy's Festival (Tango no Sekku) on May 5 by enjoying a Sweet Flag Bath (shōbu-yu). Etymology of the Word Calamus The Latin word calamus has cognates in Greek (kalamos, meaning reed) and Sanskrit (kalama, meaning reed, pen, and a type of rice). This suggests that the term predates these languages and originates from their common ancestor, Proto-Indo-European. The Arabic word qalam (meaning pen) is likely borrowed from one of these languages or directly from Indo-European roots. From the Latin root calamus, several modern English words have evolved: Calamari: Derived from the Latin calamarium (meaning ink horn or pen case), as reeds were once used as writing implements. Calumet: Another term for the Native American peace pipe, often made from a hollow reed. Shawm: A medieval oboe-like instrument, whose sound is produced by a vibrating reed mouthpiece. Chalumeau register: Refers to the lower notes of a clarinet's range, another reed instrument.
